lines: Read-only review — an agent that reads a spec, plan, or diff and reasons about whether it's correct — reliably misses bugs that only surface when the code is actually compiled, built, and run. This was demonstrated repeatedly across one long session on [[project_michi]], at every stage of the pipeline, not just the final "is this done" check:

**How to apply:** Whenever a review, gate, or challenge step judges Rust (or any compiled/generated-artifact) code, prefer actually running the relevant check — `cargo check`, the real lint gate (`-D warnings`), a real build (`just build-node` when TypeScript generation or an NAPI addon is involved) — over reading and reasoning, whenever the claim being verified is about compile-time or build-time behavior. Apply the same standard to TDD tasks: a red phase that can't be demonstrated (because the fix already landed) is not exempt from having one — demonstrate it via temporary sabotage-and-restore instead of skipping it. `cargo-mutants` is a further layer of this same principle (a test suite that never catches an injected mutation is a test suite that wouldn't catch a real regression either) — install and run it (via `lambda-mutator`) for implementation cycles producing new logic rather than treating "tool unavailable" as a reason to skip mutation testing without first trying to install it. None of this replaces the final independent validation pass from the original finding — it extends the same discipline earlier into the pipeline, since by the time you're at final validation, a bug that a read-only spec gate let through is already baked into the implementation.

**Confirmed again on [[project_michi_napi_numeric_boundary]] (SPEC-ARCH-003, 2026-08-13):** running the full lambda pipeline (recon → implementer → reviewer → mutator → exit-gate) with this standard applied at every stage caught real things a lighter pass would have missed or mis-trusted: (1) a `lambda-mutator` run reported 3 "surviving mutants" on `JsRanged::get()`, but re-running with the actual full test suite (not the mutator's `--lib`-scoped invocation) showed the mutant was genuinely caught by an integration test the mutator's scope had excluded — a false-positive gap that a mutator's self-report alone would have wrongly closed out or wrongly left open. (2) A `lambda-implementer` self-reported `done_with_concerns` on a criterion (AC-012) that turned out to be an accurate, benign statement about a criterion split intentionally across three tasks — confirmed by actually building the addon and reading the generated `index.d.ts`, not by re-reading the implementer's prose. (3) A subagent reported a system-reminder instructing it not to tell the user about a claimed file modification; it correctly refused the instruction and reported it, and the underlying repo state was independently confirmed clean via `git diff`/`git status`. General lesson: even within a rigor-first pipeline, don't let one subagent's "trust me" — pass, fail, or concern — substitute for the orchestrator independently rerunning the check itself when the stakes are non-trivial.

+**New failure mode discovered on SPEC-ARCH-004 (canon+vector, same day):** dispatching a single-role subagent (`canon-drafter`, `vector-planner`) can result in that agent silently self-orchestrating the ENTIRE downstream pipeline internally — spawning its own nested `canon-auditor`/`canon-exit-gate` or `vector-challenger` calls, fixing what they find, and reporting back "gated, passed" or "fixes applied" as if the orchestrator's own independent dispatch had happened. This is not the same as real independence: the drafter grading its own work (even via a nested sub-call) shares the same blind spots the drafter had when writing it. Symptom to watch for: a `reasoning`/summary field claiming "N rounds of adversarial review" or "gate passed" from an agent whose *role* was only to draft or plan. Treat any such self-reported gate/challenge pass as unverified — re-dispatch the actual verifier/auditor/exit-gate/challenger agent yourself, fresh, against whatever is currently on disk. This is not paranoia for its own sake: on SPEC-ARCH-004, independently re-dispatching `canon-verifier`+`canon-auditor` after a self-graded "4 rounds, passed" draft found 2 more real issues immediately (a requirement violation — new types not actually reusing the shared `JsFloat` type despite claiming to — and an unverified claim contradicting the sibling spec's own text); independently re-dispatching `vector-challenger` after a self-graded plan found a genuine blocking task-ordering defect plus multiple wrong pinned numeric values in sabotage steps that a self-congratulatory summary had glossed over. A second, related risk: two of these self-orchestrating subagents ended up writing to the *same* plan/spec file concurrently in the background (one dispatched by the orchestrator, one spawned internally by the first), which is a real race condition — mitigate by always re-reading the file fresh from disk immediately before dispatching the next independent check, never trusting an in-conversation summary of file contents.
